title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
methodology: Theoretical: Input-output network model; Hulten's theorem extension; spectral analysis of Leontief matrix; sector-level Domar weights
dataset_used: US BEA Input-Output Tables (1972–1997); 400 sectors
main_findings: Idiosyncratic shocks aggregate into macro fluctuations when network is non-symmetric; cascade effects travel through upstream-downstream linkages; volatility decay is determined by network topology, not law of large numbers
limitations: Static model; fixed input-output coefficients; no firm-level heterogeneity; no financial frictions

title: Supply Chain Disruptions: Evidence from the Great East Japan Earthquake
methodology: Causal: Difference-in-differences using spatial exogeneity of earthquake; GE production network model; upstream/downstream propagation estimation
dataset_used: Interfirm transaction network (RIETI Japan), ~1M firm pairs; firm-level sales/output data 2009–2012; Geographic disaster damage data
main_findings: Earthquake caused −0.47 pp Japan GDP; shocks propagated both upstream and downstream beyond tier-1; indirect effects larger than direct; network topology determines amplification magnitude
limitations: Japan-specific institutional context; does not model substitution across suppliers over time; single country

title: Systemic Risk and Stability in Financial Networks
methodology: Theoretical: Network model of interbank liabilities; phase-transition analysis; shock magnitude threshold analysis
dataset_used: Stylized financial networks (ring, complete, and arbitrary structure) calibrated to interbank exposure data
main_findings: Financial contagion exhibits phase transition: dense networks are stabilizing for small shocks but amplify large shocks; "robust-yet-fragile" structure; beyond threshold, interconnection spreads rather than absorbs shocks
limitations: Stylized network topology; static; no dynamics post-default; limited empirical calibration

title: Systemic Risk in Banking Ecosystems
methodology: Ecological analogy: Food-web network stability models applied to banking; SIR-like epidemiological diffusion on financial networks; complexity-stability tradeoff analysis
dataset_used: Stylized financial network inspired by Bank of England balance sheet data; topology experiments
main_findings: Financial networks exhibit same complexity-fragility dynamics as ecological food webs; diversity of institutions reduces correlation risk; homogenization of bank balance sheets raised systemic fragility pre-2008; policy lesson: targeted buffers for systemically important nodes
limitations: Highly stylized; no empirical calibration against actual bank data; does not model liquidity or fire-sale dynamics

title: The Macroeconomics of Epidemics
methodology: SEIR-macro hybrid: SIR epidemiological model embedded in standard macro model; rational agents choose consumption/labor to reduce infection risk; competitive equilibrium vs. social optimum
dataset_used: US COVID-19 infection, hospitalization, and fatality data (2020); US macro aggregates (NIPA, BLS)
main_findings: Pandemic acts as simultaneous supply-demand shock; rational agents endogenously reduce consumption/work, worsening recession; social optimum saves ~500K US lives vs. competitive equilibrium; containment policy trades recession depth for lives saved
limitations: Rational expectations assumption during acute crisis; no financial sector; homogeneous agents; no trade channel

title: Financial Contagion
methodology: Theoretical: Diamond-Dybvig banking model extended to networks; incomplete vs. complete interbank market structures; liquidity shock contagion equilibrium model
dataset_used: Stylized interbank network (ring and complete graph); abstract region structure
main_findings: First formal equilibrium model of financial contagion; incomplete interbank structures are fragile — small regional shocks cascade; complete networks more robust than incomplete; contagion is an equilibrium, not a market failure per se
limitations: Three-region stylized model; no empirical application; abstracts from asset price dynamics and fire sales

title: Liaisons Dangereuses: Increasing Connectivity, Risk Sharing, and Systemic Risk
authors: Battiston, Delli Gatti, Gallegati, Greenwald, Stiglitz
methodology: ABM/stochastic: Coupled stochastic processes for individual financial robustness; credit network with financial accelerator; default cascade; Monte Carlo simulation of systemic default probability
dataset_used: Stylized credit network; Monte Carlo experiments over varying density parameters
main_findings: Financial network is most resilient at intermediate connectivity, not maximal; financial accelerator makes individual fragility self-reinforcing; above connectivity threshold, default risk (individual and systemic) increases; diversification has non-monotonic systemic effects
limitations: Highly stylized; no empirical network data; financial accelerator assumed, not derived

title: Financial Networks and Contagion
methodology: Network theory: Graph-theoretic cascade model; integration and diversification as network parameters; discontinuous threshold failures; comparative statics on cascade extent
dataset_used: European sovereign debt cross-holdings matrix (2012 EBA stress tests); stylized organization networks
main_findings: Integration and diversification have nonmonotonic effects: initial diversification enables cascades, then prevents them; integration increases exposure to partners while reducing own-investment sensitivity; regime changes in cascade size with network parameters
limitations: Static model; no dynamic adjustment; no endogenous recovery or policy response

title: The Building Blocks of Economic Complexity
methodology: Network science: Bipartite country-product export network; method of reflections (iterative algorithm); ECI and PCI derived from eigenvectors of incidence matrix
dataset_used: SITC Rev. 2 bilateral trade data (1962–2000); 128 countries, 779 products (threshold: >$1M, >0.1% world exports)
main_findings: ECI predicts future GDP growth better than standard macro variables; countries converge to income levels dictated by complexity; deviations from ECI-income relation predict growth; product space constrains economic diversification paths
limitations: Export data only (no services); RCA threshold introduces binary classification; method of reflections convergence issues in sparse networks

title: The Granular Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
methodology: Granularity theory: Power-law firm size distribution; idiosyncratic shock aggregation with fat-tailed size distribution; Compustat data calibration; cross-sector variance decomposition
dataset_used: Compustat US firm-level data; 100 largest US firms; BEA output data 1951–2008
main_findings: Top 100 US firms explain ~1/3 of output variation and Solow residual; fat-tailed size distribution means idiosyncratic shocks don't average out; granularity hypothesis provides microfoundation for aggregate productivity shocks
limitations: US-centric; firm-level data quality dependent on Compustat coverage; macro identification challenges

title: Cascading Failures in Production Networks
journal: NBER Working Paper / ERN Input-Output Models
methodology: Theoretical: Production network model with extensive margin (firm entry/exit); endogenous systemic importance; non-divisibility-driven avalanche dynamics
dataset_used: BEA Input-Output Tables; firm-level productivity shock calibration
main_findings: Canonical I-O models miss cascade amplification because they lack entry/exit margin; firm systemic importance is endogenous to shocks and depends on role as both supplier and customer; non-divisibilities in systemic industries can trigger large-scale avalanches from a single failure
limitations: Working paper (no published version as of 2026); no empirical calibration outside US; limited tractability for general network topologies

title: Microeconomic Origins of Macroeconomic Tail Risks
methodology: Non-linear network theory: Hulten theorem extended beyond first order; network-mediated amplification of microeconomic shocks; tail risk derivation from Domar weights and shock distributions
dataset_used: BEA US Input-Output Tables; sectoral TFP shocks (1948–2014)
main_findings: Micro shock distributions + network topology generate fat-tailed macro output distributions; negative shocks amplified, positive attenuated (negative skewness); average output losses from sectoral shocks are order-of-magnitude larger than Lucas welfare cost; 1970s oil shock impact tripled by network
limitations: Assumes efficient equilibria; limited empirical identification of shock distributions; US-only calibration

title: Distortions in Production Networks
methodology: Input-output with distortions: Static GE network model; Hulten-like theorem for distortions via TFP and labor wedge channels; Domar weights as sufficient statistics
dataset_used: US BEA I-O Tables (2007–2009); financial distortion proxies (credit spreads, sector-level lending data) from 2008 crisis
main_findings: US I-O network amplified 2008 financial distortions by factor ~2; near efficiency, distortions affect labor wedge (not TFP) based on sector network centrality; Domar weights are sufficient statistics for distortion propagation
limitations: Static framework; does not model dynamics or financial sector structure explicitly; US-specific

title: Firm-Level Propagation of Shocks Through Supply-Chain Networks
methodology: Agent-based model: ~1M Japanese firm-level supply-chain network; Monte Carlo simulation of 30 initial-condition replicates; parameter calibration to actual post-earthquake production dynamics
dataset_used: Actual supplier-customer network of 1M Japanese firms (Tokyo Shoko Research); regional production data 2010–2012; Nankai earthquake risk scenarios
main_findings: Indirect production loss from supply-chain propagation (10.6% GDP for Nankai scenario) vastly exceeds direct damage (0.5%); scale-free networks amplify more than random; low input substitutability and network cycles amplify persistence; hub firms drive propagation speed
limitations: Japan-specific network; agent behavior rules simplistic; no financial or price channels

title: Modeling Loss-Propagation in the Global Supply Network: The Dynamic Agent-Based Model Acclimate
methodology: Dynamic ABM: National sectors as agents in global supply network; demand/supply adjustment rules; warehousing and idle capacity buffers; disaster-induced production loss propagation
dataset_used: OECD ICIO (2011, 45 sectors, 43 countries); stylized disaster scenarios (location, magnitude, duration)
main_findings: Indirect global losses comparable in size to direct disaster losses; warehousing and idle capacity efficiently mitigate propagation; first-tier supplier focus is insufficient — full supply chain assessment required; code open-source on GitHub
limitations: Simplified agent decision rules; no price dynamics; no financial sector; ICIO data lag of 3–4 years

title: Input Specificity and the Propagation of Idiosyncratic Shocks in Production Networks
methodology: Causal: Natural experiment (US natural disasters 1978–2013); difference-in-differences on supplier-customer sales growth; input specificity as heterogeneous treatment variable
dataset_used: Compustat supplier-customer links (~7,000 pairs); NOAA natural disaster declarations 1978–2013; BEA sector-level input specificity measures
main_findings: Supplier disaster reduces customer sales by ~2 pp; effect scales with input specificity (non-substitutable inputs propagate more); spills over to other suppliers; point estimates economically large
limitations: US listed firms only (Compustat bias); disaster identification requires size threshold; limited downstream propagation analysis

title: Input Linkages and the Transmission of Shocks: Firm-Level Evidence from the 2011 Tōhoku Earthquake
methodology: Causal: Multinational firm natural experiment; Leontief elasticity estimation; CMF microdata + Census of Manufactures
dataset_used: US Census of Manufactures (CMF) + Longitudinal Business Database (LBD); 2010–2012 Japanese import data; Japanese affiliate indicator
main_findings: US affiliates of Japanese multinationals had one-for-one output-import drops post-earthquake; cross-country shock transmission through input linkages is large; global supply chains sufficiently rigid to play important macroeconomic transmission role
limitations: Limited to US-Japan MNC bilateral pairs; elasticity estimates may not generalize to non-MNC relationships; short-run analysis

title: Shock Propagation on Global Trade-Investment Multiplex Networks
methodology: Network science: Multiplex network model (trade + FDI layers); spreading dynamics combining inter-country contagion and intra-country distress propagation; network vulnerability analysis
dataset_used: UN Comtrade bilateral trade data; UNCTAD FDI bilateral stock data; multiplex topology metrics
main_findings: Trade and financial interactions interact to influence country vulnerability; high-FDI countries have amplified trade shock vulnerability; simple linear relation between relative economic distress and effective network centrality at large scale
limitations: No distinction between gross/value-added trade; FDI data quality varies; dynamics simplified

title: Crisis Contagion in the World Trade Network
methodology: Google PageRank matrix analysis of world trade network; bankruptcy threshold κ governing phase transition; trade balance-linked contagion
dataset_used: UN Comtrade bilateral trade flows (1962–2019); 227 countries
main_findings: On-off phase transition: below threshold κc, crisis is global (~90% country bankruptcies); above, confined to <10%; Western economies (Old Continent, US/Mexico) are systemic sources; BRIC nations most robust; Australia late-stage resistance
limitations: Stylized bankruptcy model; no price or financial mechanisms; no agent heterogeneity

title: Aggregate Fluctuations in Adaptive Production Networks
methodology: Dynamic ABM: Firm exit/entry + supplier search with switching costs and search frictions; firm-level international supply-network data calibration
dataset_used: Large international firm-level production network dataset (FactSet/Orbis); sector-level switching costs from procurement surveys
main_findings: Reshoring reduces output and increases volatility; network adaptivity amplifies volatility via search frictions; firm exit propagates via supplier loss; restricting buyer-supplier links is counterproductive for resilience
limitations: Firm-level international data quality/coverage variable; switching cost estimation indirect

title: Country Size, International Trade, and Aggregate Fluctuations in Granular Economies
methodology: Quantitative general equilibrium: Multi-country model with heterogeneous firms; power-law size distribution; firm-level simulation calibrated to 50 largest economies
dataset_used: Compustat global + WorldScope firm data; BvD Amadeus; UN Comtrade; 50 largest economies by GDP
main_findings: Trade increases macro volatility 15–20% in small open economies; smaller countries have fewer large firms and higher volatility; trade opening amplifies large firms' importance thus raising systemic exposure
limitations: Abstracting from financial channels; firm data incomplete for many developing countries; model abstracts from services trade

title: Technology, Geography, and Trade
methodology: Ricardian GE model: Continuous goods with Fréchet productivity distribution; bilateral trade gravity from first principles; structural gravity estimation; iceberg trade cost parameterization
dataset_used: Bilateral manufacturing trade flows; price data; geographic distance/barriers; 19 OECD countries 1990
main_findings: Structural gravity model; trade costs estimated at ~170% ad-valorem equivalent; gains from trade ~10%; model predicts observed trade patterns well; foundational methodology for all quantitative trade models
limitations: 19 OECD countries only; no intermediate goods; no services; assumes balanced trade

title: The Impact of Regional and Sectoral Productivity Changes on the U.S. Economy
methodology: Quantitative spatial-sectoral GE model: 50 US states × 26 sectors; interregional and intersectoral trade; I-O matrix linkages; labor mobility; counterfactual simulations
dataset_used: US BEA I-O Tables; QCEW regional employment; Census Bureau trade flows by state-industry; Annual Survey of Manufactures
main_findings: Katrina hurricane: Louisiana infrastructure shock propagated nationally via I-O linkages; California computer boom had national productivity spillovers; spatial + sectoral elasticities vary significantly; I-O structure is key amplifier
limitations: US only; annual frequency; no financial frictions; labor mobility is simplified

title: Contagion in Financial Networks
journal: Bank of England Working Paper 383 (published: Proceedings of the Royal Society A 466(2120):2401–2423, 2010)
methodology: Network contagion model: Arbitrary network structure; generating function approach; liquidity hoarding and asset market feedback; probability/impact analysis
dataset_used: UK interbank network data (stylized topology); Monte Carlo simulations of interbank exposure matrices
main_findings: Financial systems exhibit "robust-yet-fragile" property: low probability of contagion, but widespread when triggered; network connectivity and asset illiquidity interact; pre-2007 resilience should not be taken as future guide; heterogeneous network structure produces fat tails
limitations: Working paper version differs from published Royal Society A version; stylized network; no dynamic adjustment

title: Cascade Effects of Global Supply Chains Induced by Regional Conflicts Increase Global Inequality
methodology: Geographic I-O model: OECD ICIO extended geographically; Russia-Ukraine grain shock simulation; sector-level production loss and cascading pattern estimation; Monte Carlo confidence intervals (95% CI)
dataset_used: OECD ICIO; FAO agricultural production statistics; Russia-Ukraine bilateral trade data (2021); sector-level grain supply data
main_findings: Textile sector suffered highest cascading losses (17.04% ± 0.72%); food-processing: 16.85% ± 0.5%; dual propagation chains: grain-food/livestock and light-heavy manufacturing; low-income countries disproportionately affected; conflict amplifies pre-existing inequality
limitations: Short time horizon; static I-O assumptions; Russia-Ukraine specific shock size assumptions
